intent: Summarize the tradeoffs between HNSW and IVFFlat indexes in pgvector and recommend one for a 1M-row knowledge base.

plan_steps.description: Gather the recall/latency/build-time characteristics of HNSW and IVFFlat.
plan_steps.expected_output: Both indexes' key tradeoffs identified with sources.

plan_steps.description: Make a recommendation tied to the 1M-row, read-heavy constraint.

step_results.output: HNSW: higher recall and lower query latency, slower build, more memory. IVFFlat: cheaper to build, lower memory, recall depends on probes and requires training on representative data.
For 1M rows that are read-heavy with infrequent writes, HNSW is recommended: the one-time build cost is amortized and query latency/recall dominate.

final_output: Recommendation: use HNSW for the 1M-row read-heavy KB. HNSW gives higher recall and lower query latency than IVFFlat at the cost of a slower, more memory-intensive build; since writes are infrequent that build cost is amortized. Choose IVFFlat only if memory is tightly constrained or rebuilds are frequent.

intent: Compare the MIT and Apache-2.0 licenses for a self-hosted open-source project, focusing on patent grants.

plan_steps.description: State the core permissions and conditions of each license.
Highlight the patent-grant difference and its practical impact.
plan_steps.expected_output: Explains Apache-2.0's explicit patent grant vs MIT's silence.

step_results.output: MIT: permissive, requires preserving the copyright notice, no explicit patent terms. Apache-2.0: permissive, requires NOTICE preservation, includes an explicit patent license and termination clause.
Apache-2.0 grants contributors' patent rights to users and terminates them on patent litigation; MIT is silent on patents, leaving an implied (weaker, jurisdiction-dependent) grant.

final_output: Both MIT and Apache-2.0 are permissive. The key difference for patents: Apache-2.0 includes an explicit patent grant plus a retaliation/termination clause, giving downstream users clearer protection; MIT says nothing about patents, relying on a weaker implied grant. For a project where contributors may hold patents, Apache-2.0 is the safer default.
